newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Buyers seek bargains in Russian preference shares.
newsitem.headline: Buyers seek bargains in Russian preference shares.

text.p: Bargain-hunting investors, seeking dividend income or an arbitrage opportunity, are increasingly buying preference shares in Russian blue chip stocks, traders and analysts said on Monday.
Preference shares in five top firms have been listed on the Russian Trading System electronic over-the-counter network since the beginning of this month and dealers say volume is growing.

"Some people make the calculation that they do not have significant voting power in blue chip companies, so why not go for dividend yield ?" said Jim Nail, equity analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Moscow.

Preference shares, which give investors a priority dividend but do not carry voting rights, make up 25 percent of most Russian companies' capital. They were often shares originally handed to workers and management when the firm was privatised.
Most company charters give 10 percent of net income as preference share dividends.
Nail said some people also hoped the preference shares, which typically trade at 40-60 percent of the ordinary share price, would be converted into common stock.
"If you were really lucky, you would get a great dividend yield for two years and then a real windfall when they were converted because of the lower price of the preference shares."
The five prefs listed on the RTS are in Unified Energy System, Norilsk Nickel and in three oil companies -- Noyabrskneftegaz, Surgutneftegaz and Yuganskneftegaz.
UES ordinary shares were at $0.788/$0.794 on the RTS in mid-afternoon with 16.35 million shares traded while the preference shares were at $0.0405/$0.0428 with 716,000 traded.
Norilsk Nickel ordinaries were at $7.21/$7.35 and preference shares stood at $3.50/$3.75 with 20,000 of each traded.
Liquidity in the stocks, though growing, is still far lower than in ordinary shares. "It is not something people do who are interested in being able to get in and out quickly," Nail said.
Herman Zvezdin, equity salesman at Troika-Dialog, said other popular preference shares not on the list include Lenenergo, Moscow telephone company MGTS and Russia's biggest oil company LUKoil.
Dirk Damrau, head of research at Renaissance Capital, said preference shares were becoming more interesting as the economy picked up and the prospect of payouts increased.
"There is justification for them becoming more interesting, especially for investors who are looking around and saying 'what can I buy at the moment?'"
But Renaissance said in a weekly market review on Monday that investors should look at individual oil preference shares.
It said dividends were not a sufficient reason to invest. Payment was often delayed and the rouble-denominated dividend could be eroded by the time it was paid in hard currency.
The review also said the big oil groups firms effectively control their listed units and would be unlikely to agree to convert preference shares into ordinary voting stocks.
This would make capital appreciation on the preference shares less likely. The wider bid-ask spreads, of 20-40 percent, on preference shares would make it harder to realise gains.
Renaissance sees two key exceptions. LUKoil's plans to issue American Depositary Receipts should improve liquidity, thus helping cut spreads and close the arbitrage gap.

The management of the AO Surgutneftegaz production unit is the same as in the NK Surgutneftegaz holding company, so would be less concerned about the effect of consolidation on control and probably keener to cut dividend payments.
"There is clearly an arbitrage that will be gradually worked out, a discount that should not necessarily be there," said Damrau. "But you should look at it on a company-by-company basis."
